headline: The Missile Defense Agency has awarded Lockheed Martin a $211.4 million contract modification to build new Configuration 3 (C3) THAAD launchers for the United Arab Emirates (UAE) under a Foreign Military Sales (FMS) agreement. The move is intended to strengthen the UAE’s ballistic missile defense capability while allowing its THAAD launchers to be more widely dispersed across the country. The significance of Configuration 3 goes beyond simply adding more launchers. It is part of THAAD’s broader hardware and software modernization, bringing improvements to cybersecurity and Link 16 communications while enhancing the system’s ability to integrate with a wider range of sensors. This is particularly important for the UAE, where key targets, including air bases, ports, population centers, energy facilities, and logistics infrastructure, are spread across a relatively large area. Recent regional missile attacks have demonstrated that effective interception is only part of the equation. Maintaining sufficient interceptor reserves and the ability to sustain defensive operations through multiple attack waves are equally critical. With the growing threat from ballistic missiles, cruise missiles, and drones across the Middle East, the UAE is moving toward a more dispersed, interconnected, and resilient air defense architecture.

headline: RT by @sentdefender: An Italian Eurofighter assigned to NATO’s Baltic Air Policing mission shot down a drone of unconfirmed, but likely Russian origin after it entered Latvian airspace Friday, according to NATO and Latvian authorities. Two Italian Eurofighters scrambled from Lithuania along with two Turkish F-16s from Estonia. One of the Italian jets identified and engaged the drone. Latvian forces are now searching for the wreckage near Rugāji, about 35 km from the Russian border, so the drone’s origin has not yet been established. The incident comes amid a growing number of drone incursions into Baltic airspace. Latvia says Ukrainian drones have entered the region several times this year, while officials also point to Russian electronic warfare as a possible factor causing Ukrainian systems to stray across borders. Before Friday's incident, Ukrainian forces had launched attacks against Russian ports near St. Petersburg. Russian authorities claimed to have intercepted 15 Ukrainian drones during those attacks. This is the third reported NATO interception of a drone in the Baltics in recent months, following a Romanian F-16 shootdown in Estonia in May and a French Rafale shootdown in Latvia in June.

headline: The Trump administration has asked the Supreme Court to allow construction of the White House’s $400 million ballroom to continue while it appeals a lower court ruling that halted the project, according to the Associated Press. The D.C. Circuit ruled 2-1 that Trump cannot proceed without congressional approval, finding that the president lacks unilateral authority to build the 90,000 square foot structure where the East Wing once stood. The administration argues the project is necessary for White House security, calling the injunction unlawful and warning that stopping construction would leave an active construction site that is harder to secure. The appeals court had exempted work necessary for White House safety. The Supreme Court is being asked to act before the lower court's ruling takes effect on Aug. 21. The administration says the project is already about 65% complete after 10 months of construction.

headline: The U.S. is reportedly asking NATO allies to document not just their defense spending, but their political alignment with the Trump administration as part of its review of the U.S. military presence in Europe, according to reporting from Bloomberg. A questionnaire sent to NATO members asks whether governments have been publicly supportive of U.S. foreign policy, restricted U.S. military access to their bases, purchased from U.S. defense contractors, or opposed Euro-preference procurement rules. It specifically references restrictions imposed by allies on U.S. operations in the Middle East and asks whether those restrictions could be reduced or eliminated. The questionnaire comes as Washington considers major reductions to U.S. forces and wartime capabilities in Europe, with the review expected to conclude by December. Allies reportedly view the questions as an attempt to link U.S. security guarantees to political loyalty, potentially marking a significant shift from the traditional NATO model, where collective defense has been maintained despite political disagreements among members.

headline: U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) has issued a 'fact check' to correct what it describes as a series of false reports about conditions aboard the Nimitz class aircraft carrier USS Abraham Lincoln (CVN-72), including claims that seven sailors died in a fight aboard the ship and reports of increased suicidal ideations among the crew. According to the Navy, no service members aboard Abraham Lincoln have died during its current deployment, and the sailor who went overboard on August 3 was quickly and safely recovered. The carrier strike group has now spent more than 260 days at sea, conducting more than 10,000 aircraft flights and expending approximately 1.5 million pounds of ordnance. The Navy also says Abraham Lincoln has maintained an 84.4% crew reenlistment rate, among the highest of any U.S. aircraft carrier. headline: President Donald J. Trump has issued a memorandum directing a major overhaul of U.S. Navy shipbuilding, citing cost growth, delays, design complexity and insufficient industrial capacity. Among the key directives: • CVN-81: Within 60 days, the administration will develop a plan to replace the EMALS electromagnetic catapult system and Advanced Weapons Elevators with traditional steam and hydraulic systems. • Foreign shipbuilding: The administration will pursue a "Finland Model" allowing foreign shipbuilders to participate in up to three ship classes, provided they build or acquire a U.S. shipyard, train an American workforce, transfer relevant technology and establish a U.S. supply chain. The first two ships could be built overseas, with subsequent ships built in the United States. • New surface combatants: The Navy will develop a new competitive acquisition approach for affordable, mature-design surface combatants capable of anti-submarine warfare, surface warfare and convoy escort. • Fifth Navy shipyard: A plan will be developed for a fifth public Navy yard, including additional drydock capacity for nuclear-powered submarines and aircraft carriers. • Submarine repair: The administration will establish a Component Repair Center intended to maintain at least one complete set of spare equipment for the Los Angeles, Virginia, Seawolf, Ohio and Columbia classes. • NAVSEA reform: The Naval Sea Systems Command will undergo a review aimed at reducing bureaucracy, increasing accountability and preventing repeated redesigns of mature ship designs. The memorandum's overarching objective is to increase U.S. shipbuilding capacity and competition while reducing the cost and time required to build and maintain Navy vessels. Importantly, most of these provisions direct the Department of War and Navy to develop plans within specified timelines; they do not themselves immediately authorize or fund construction of the projects described.

headline: President Trump has directed the Navy to abandon the electromagnetic aircraft launch system (EMALS) being used on the Gerald R. Ford class carriers and return to traditional steam catapults, according to U.S. officials cited by the Wall Street Journal. Trump signed a national security memorandum directing the Navy to redesign the fourth Ford class carrier, Doris Miller, and subsequent ships around steam catapults. The first three carriers, Gerald R. Ford, John F. Kennedy and Enterprise, will retain EMALS. The decision reverses years of Navy and industry resistance to Trump's proposal, largely because replacing EMALS would require significant redesign and could cost billions of dollars. Trump has criticized EMALS for years, arguing that it is overly complex and less reliable than steam catapults. The move effectively locks in a major technological reversal for future U.S. aircraft carriers.
